newsitem.title: UK: Nigerian ban shadows quiet ex-UK-Africa air market.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian ban shadows quiet ex-UK-Africa air market.

text.p: The tit-for-tat British-Nigerian ban on each others aircraft is dominating talk in the ex-UK to Nigeria air cargo, a Reuters survey showed.
Traditionally May and June are relatively quiet months in the UK-Africa market and market activity appears to be in line with expectations.
British carriers are still eagerly awaiting the lifting of the Nigerian ban on all British-registered flights into the country, imposed on May 16.
Carriers do not seem to be to hopeful that the situation will be resolved quickly as the ban entered its fourth week and inter-governmental talks continued, said industry sources.
The British Department of Transport is trying to send inspectors to Nigeria to inspect Nigerian aircraft that would be used on the UK route but currently visas are being denied.
If the Civil Aviation Authority inspectors can carry out an inspection, the government is confident the situation can be resolved, said a government spokeswoman.
Attempts are being made to find a third country where the inspection could take place or somewhere in the UK that is not near any population centres, she added.
A British Airways spokesman said the situation appears to be stalemate.

Under its usual schedule BA operates a daily B747 flight to Lagos and a three-times-weekly DC-10 service to Kano which travels on to Accra in Ghana. Kano has been by-passed, although the service to Accra continues.
The Nigerian government imposed the ban following the British government's move to bar Nigerian flights two months previously on safety grounds.
DHL 's area manager for West Africa, Edward Bellord, told Reuters by telephone from Abidjan that the ban had reduced capacity on the Lagos-London route by two wide-body aircraft a day.

The express operator had to implement contingency plans for southbound uplift from Europe which is a problem, he said. UK business accounts for approximately 25 percent of DHL's inbound Nigerian air express business, he said.
The express operator is using carriers such as Lufthansa via Frankfurt and Sabena through DHL's European hub in Brussels and KLM via Amsterdam.
DHL is also using Air Afrique into Abidjan and transhipping on to Lagos, which can result in delays of 24-hours, he added.
The express company is looking into the possibility of operating dedicated charters between Lagos and its West Africa hub in Abidjan.
DHL is in talks with Air Afrique and other African carriers and expects to make a final decision on the charter operation and type of aircraft to be used in the next five days.
This would only be to supplement uplift when DHL could not get enough capacity from the other carriers flying into Nigeria, he stressed.
He added that DHL had not lost any business into Nigeria, although cargo is subject to delays, he added.
Colin Carr, director of Nigeria Airways' NIA.CN UK cargo GSA Air Sea Broker, said May and June are usually quiet to Nigeria.
As part of its contingency plans, Nigerian cargo is being put on another of the company's customers - MK Airlines.
MK Airlines, fortunately is a Ghanaian cargo carrier, so Nigerian destined cargo is being flown into Ghana and transhipped on to Lagos, added Carr.
However, he said that the London-Lagos route is usually both highly competitive and a low-rate market because of the large amount of capacity available by both charter and scheduled carriers.
Rates are holding firm at 0.97 per kg to Lagos.

Ghana, on the other hand, tends to be more steady with prospects for the economy looking good, said Carr. The stable economy does mean that investment and business confidence is high, industry observers commented.
However, competition is a factor in the Ghanaian market as well, with carriers such as BA, KLM, Lufthansa and Alitalia all operating there.
Also Ghana Airways introduced a fourth weekly service to Accra from London on May 4. The DC-10 adds another 15 tonnes capacity to the route.

David Hall spokesman for A.N.A. Aviation Services the cargo gsas of several African carriers including Air Afrique, Affretair, Air Gabon and DAS Air amongst others, said that the Nigerian ban boosted cargo levels initially when it was first put in place.
Gabon, especially, is a very stable market, he said. Air Gabon operates weekly Boeing 747 combis on the route with approximately 20 tonnes a flight being sent to Libreville and Johannesburg.

Much of the cargo is destined for South Africa but the many oil exploration projects going on in the region are stimulating demand. Oil equipment is a major cargo to Libreville, Port Gentil and Pointe-Noire.
Freetown in Sierra Leone has been very busy in the last few weeks, he said and the company is even expecting Kinshasa to come back on line again soon for Air Gabon.
DAS Air, a Ugandan-registered carrier, which operates Boeing 707 freighters from London Gatwick will be introducing a second DC-10 on October 2, he said.
As well as operating to Africa ex-UK, the carrier also operates from the Middle East including Bahrain, Abu Dhabi, and Dubai.
It flies form both Europe and Dubai to Entebbe which is where it has a bonded warehouse. The second DC-10 is being converted into a freighter by Italian company Alenia.
DAS Air has been very busy bringing in cobalt from Zambia to Rotterdam and Antwerp on its existing DC-10F and two Boeing 707 freighters.
A spokesman from Air Zimbabwe said that the market is relatively stable but very much seasonal. Around 90 percent of exports from the country are perishables such as beans and strawberries, he said.

Several projects are stimulating the market such as the upgrading of Harare airport and some hydro-electric projects. Also many tobacco manufacturers also buy British equipment, said industry observers.
Kenya Airways' UK cargo manager Jeffrey Fish said that it too is a market that does fluctuate with the seasons but currently it is fairly steady.
Major exports from the UK are industrial, agricultural and mining equipment, he said. Kenya is a popular export destination but it often still has too much capacity.

Rates from the UK to African destinations do seem to have edged upwards, though only slightly. London Accra stands at 0.97 stg per kg up from 0.95 per kg, Entebbe is averaging at 1.00 per kg. Harare is slightly up to 1.45 per kg from 1.43 stg a kg. Johannesburg has remained static at 1.55 per kg. Libreville can apparently vary the most, from 2.20 stg per kg to 3.00 stg per kg depending on whether using French or British carriers, industry sources said.
